name: Leek hair dye

card.summary: A plant-based hair colouring from ancient Rome in which leek preparations were used to darken grey hair, an early example of natural dye used to change hair colour.
card.note: Historical practice; no modern product or trial.

quick.overview:
Leek hair dye refers to ancient preparations made from leeks, recorded in Roman sources as a way to darken or recolour hair. Its appearance payoff was masking grey and achieving the fashionable darker shade.

Accounts describe a decoction of the leek outer coat, and encyclopedia entries describe a black dye of leeks and boiled walnuts. No modern studies have tested it.
quick.how: Historically, leek parts were boiled and the liquid applied to hair. Modern use is rare and mostly of historical interest.
quick.risks: No modern safety data exists. Plant dyes can cause skin allergy in some people, and the practice is not a regulated cosmetic product.

lead: Leek hair dye is an ancient Roman plant-based hair colouring. A passage in Pliny the Elder's Natural History, as reported in secondary sources, describes a decoction of the outer coat of the leek acting as a dye on grey hair.[3]

Roman hair fashion ran from blond, popular and associated with Gaul and Germany, to red and black, and many Romans reportedly preferred a black dye of leeks and boiled walnuts.[2] The appeal of such dyes was disguising grey and changing colour using kitchen and garden plants.
Leeks are listed among ancient plant-derived hair dyes alongside henna, indigo and walnut hulls.[1] No published modern trial has examined leek preparations as a hair colourant.

chain: Leek outer coat boiled into a liquid
Darker, more uniform hair colour (as historically described)
angle.text: In ancient Rome, leek-based preparations were used to darken grey hair. Sources describe the effect qualitatively; no measured results exist.

paras: Plant-based hair dyes date back millennia; examples include Egyptian recipes in the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) and Assyrian recipes.[1] Roman fashion favoured blond, red and black shades, with gold dust available to the very wealthy.[2] Leek preparations belong to the dark-dye tradition: a decoction of the leek outer coat for grey hair, and a leek-and-walnut black dye.[2][3]

timeline.event: Ebers Papyrus records dye recipes for grey hair.[1]
Pliny the Elder's Natural History mentions a leek decoction as a dye for grey hair.[3]
